sections.title: Introduction to Control Systems Security
sections.description: Defining control system cybersecurity, trends, potential consequences, malware events, and differences between IT and IACS
learningObjectives: Describe the need and importance for control system security
Discuss current trends in control system cybersecurity and how they could affect control systems
Analyse the differences between IT and IACS cybersecurity
Identify potential consequences of cybersecurity breaches in control systems
Recognize malware events and their impact on critical infrastructure

topics.title: Defining Control System Cybersecurity
topics.definition: Control system cybersecurity is the practice of protecting computer systems and networks that control critical infrastructure from unauthorized access, attacks, and damage.
topics.explanation: Control systems manage essential services like power plants, water treatment facilities, and manufacturing processes. Protecting these systems is critical because failures can have severe consequences for public safety, economic stability, and national security.
keyPoints: Control systems are the backbone of critical infrastructure
Cybersecurity protects both the systems and the physical processes they control
Unlike IT systems, control systems prioritise availability and safety over confidentiality

tierCorrelations.level0: Foundation: Understanding why control systems need security
tierCorrelations.level2: Supervisory: Monitoring and controlling security measures

topics.title: Trends in Control System Cybersecurity
topics.definition: Current trends refer to emerging patterns and developments in how control systems are attacked and how security practices are evolving.
topics.explanation: The cybersecurity landscape for control systems is constantly changing. Modern trends include increased connectivity (IIoT), sophisticated nation-state attacks, ransomware targeting critical infrastructure, and the shift toward cloud-based systems. Understanding these trends helps organisations prepare for emerging threats.
keyPoints: Increased connectivity creates new attack surfaces
Sophisticated attackers are targeting critical infrastructure
Legacy systems lack modern security features
Cloud and edge computing introduce new security challenges

topics.title: IT vs IACS Cybersecurity
topics.definition: The distinction between Information Technology (IT) security and Industrial Automation and Control Systems (IACS) security based on different priorities and constraints.
topics.explanation: IT systems prioritise confidentiality and integrity, but IACS systems prioritise availability and safety. A server outage in IT might cost money, but a control system failure could cause physical harm or environmental damage. IACS also often uses older equipment that cannot be easily patched or updated.
keyPoints: IT prioritises: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability (in that order)
IACS prioritises: Availability, Safety, Integrity (in that order)
IACS systems often have long operational lifespans (20-30 years)
Downtime in IACS is often unacceptable
Legacy systems may not support modern security tools

tierCorrelations.level2: Adapting IT security practices to IACS

sections.title: Awareness
sections.description: Security awareness and the human element in cybersecurity
learningObjectives: Understand the importance of security awareness in IACS environments
Identify common security mistakes and how to prevent them

topics.title: Security Awareness Fundamentals
topics.definition: Security awareness is the understanding and knowledge that employees and stakeholders have about cybersecurity risks and best practices.
topics.explanation: Most security breaches involve human error or social engineering. Creating a culture of security awareness means training people to recognize threats, follow security policies, and report suspicious activity. This is often more effective than technical controls alone.
keyPoints: Humans are often the weakest link in security
Regular training reduces security incidents
Awareness programmes should be ongoing, not one-time
Everyone in the organisation has a role in security

sections.title: ISA/IEC 62443 Series
sections.description: Overview of the ISA/IEC 62443 standards series, its structure, and how it applies to IACS
learningObjectives: Define the purpose of each part of the ISA/IEC 62443 Series
Summarize the six main groups of standards
Understand how the standards are organized and applied
Identify which standards apply to different roles

topics.title: ISA/IEC 62443 Series Overview
topics.definition: ISA/IEC 62443 is a comprehensive series of standards developed by the International Society of Automation (ISA) and the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) to address cybersecurity in industrial automation and control systems.
topics.explanation: The series consists of multiple parts organized into six groups: General (Part 1), Policies & Procedures (Part 2), System (Part 3), and Component (Part 4) groups. Each part addresses different aspects of IACS security, from terminology and concepts to specific technical requirements.
keyPoints: 62443 is the international standard for IACS cybersecurity
It provides a comprehensive framework covering all aspects of IACS security
Standards are organized into logical groups
Different standards apply to different stakeholders (asset owners, suppliers, integrators)

tierCorrelations.level1: Knowing which standards apply to your role

topics.title: The Six Groups of Standards
topics.definition: The ISA/IEC 62443 series is organized into six main groups that address different aspects of IACS security.
topics.explanation: Group 1 (General) covers terminology and concepts. Group 2 (Policies & Procedures) addresses organisational security programmes. Group 3 (System) covers system-level security requirements. Group 4 (Component) addresses component-level security. Groups 5 and 6 cover conformance and lifecycle aspects.
keyPoints: Part 1-1: Terminology, concepts and models
Part 1-2: Master glossary of terms and definitions
Part 1-3: System security conformance metrics
Part 1-4: IACS security lifecycle and use cases
Part 2-1: Establishing an IACS security programme
Part 2-2: IACS security protection scheme
Part 3-1: Security technologies for IACS
Part 3-2: Security risk assessment for system design
Part 3-3: System security requirements and security levels

sections.title: ISA/IEC 62443 Models & Security Levels
sections.description: The Purdue Reference Model, Zone & Conduit Model, and Security Levels (SL 0-4)
learningObjectives: Explain the Purdue Reference Model and its five levels
Describe the Zone & Conduit Model and its application
Identify and explain the four Security Levels

topics.title: Purdue Reference Model
topics.definition: The Purdue Reference Model is a hierarchical framework that divides industrial automation systems into five levels based on their function and distance from physical processes.
topics.explanation: The model helps organisations understand their system architecture and apply appropriate security controls at each level. Level 0 is the process (the actual manufacturing or control happening), Level 1 is basic control devices, Level 2 is supervisory control, Level 3 is operations management, and Level 4 is enterprise systems.
keyPoints: Level 0 (Process): The actual physical process being controlled
Level 1 (Basic Control): PLCs, sensors, actuators
Level 2 (Supervisory): SCADA systems, HMIs
Level 3 (Operations): Manufacturing execution systems, real-time databases
Level 4 (Enterprise): ERP systems, business systems
Each level has different security requirements and constraints

topics.title: Zone & Conduit Model
topics.definition: The Zone & Conduit Model is a security architecture approach that groups systems into security zones and controls communication between zones through conduits.
topics.explanation: Zones are logical groupings of systems that share similar security requirements and trust levels. Conduits are the connections between zones. By controlling what can pass through conduits, organisations can prevent unauthorized access and contain breaches. This is similar to network segmentation but applied more broadly.
keyPoints: Zones group systems with similar security needs
Conduits are controlled connections between zones
Security policies are applied at zone boundaries
Reduces the attack surface by limiting communication paths
Helps contain breaches to specific zones

topics.title: Security Levels (SL 0-4)
topics.definition: Security Levels (SL) are a 0-4 scale that describes the target level of protection for an IACS system based on risk assessment.
topics.explanation: SL 0 means no specific security requirements. SL 1 protects against accidental or casual threats. SL 2 protects against intentional threats but assumes limited resources. SL 3 protects against determined threats with moderate resources. SL 4 protects against sophisticated, well-resourced threats. Organisations determine their target SL based on risk assessment.
keyPoints: SL 0: No specific security requirements
SL 1: Protection against accidental/casual threats
SL 2: Protection against intentional threats (limited resources)
SL 3: Protection against determined threats (moderate resources)
SL 4: Protection against sophisticated threats (significant resources)
Target SL is determined through risk assessment

sections.title: Intro to IACS Lifecycle
sections.description: The IACS Cybersecurity Lifecycle and its phases
learningObjectives: Identify the sub-activities of each lifecycle phase
Understand how security is integrated throughout the lifecycle
Apply lifecycle concepts to your organisation

topics.title: IACS Cybersecurity Lifecycle
topics.definition: The IACS Cybersecurity Lifecycle is a continuous process that integrates security considerations throughout the entire life of an industrial automation system.
topics.explanation: The lifecycle typically consists of three main phases: Assess (understand your current state and risks), Develop & Implement (design and deploy security measures), and Maintain (continuously monitor and improve). Unlike traditional project lifecycles that end, the cybersecurity lifecycle is continuous and iterative.
keyPoints: Phase 1 - Assess: Understand current state, identify risks, set target security levels
Phase 2 - Develop & Implement: Design security architecture, implement controls
Phase 3 - Maintain: Monitor systems, update defences, respond to incidents
The lifecycle is continuous, not a one-time project
Security must be considered from initial design through end-of-life

sections.title: Security Requirements for IACS Asset Owners
sections.description: Security programme requirements, maturity levels, and organisational responsibilities
learningObjectives: Explain the relationship between ISA/IEC 62443-2-1 and ISO/IEC 27001

topics.title: IACS Security Programme Requirements
topics.definition: A comprehensive security programme for IACS includes policies, procedures, technical controls, and organisational structures designed to protect industrial systems.
topics.explanation: Asset owners (organisations that operate IACS) are responsible for establishing and maintaining security programmes. This includes developing security policies, implementing technical controls, training personnel, and continuously monitoring and improving their security posture.
keyPoints: Security programmes must be tailored to organisational risk
Programmes should address technical, operational, and management aspects
Regular assessment and improvement are essential
Board-level commitment is necessary for programme success

sections.title: Evolving Security Standards & Practices
sections.description: Regulations, standards, frameworks, and their relationship to IACS security
learningObjectives: Compare and contrast regulations, standards, and frameworks
Analyse the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and its relation to ISA/IEC 62443

topics.title: Regulations, Standards, and Frameworks
topics.definition: Regulations are mandatory legal requirements, standards are agreed-upon specifications, and frameworks are guidance documents for implementing security practices.
topics.explanation: Different industries and countries have different regulatory requirements. Standards like ISA/IEC 62443 provide detailed technical specifications. Frameworks like NIST CSF provide high-level guidance. Organisations must understand which apply to them and how they relate to each other.
keyPoints: Regulations are legally binding (e.g., NERC CIP for power systems)
Standards provide detailed technical requirements (e.g., ISA/IEC 62443)
Frameworks provide guidance and best practices (e.g., NIST CSF)
Many standards and frameworks are complementary
Compliance requirements vary by industry and geography

topics.title: NIST Cybersecurity Framework
topics.definition: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework is a voluntary framework developed by the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology to help organisations manage cybersecurity risk.
topics.explanation: NIST CSF is organized around five functions: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover. It provides a common language for cybersecurity and helps organisations of all sizes understand and manage cybersecurity risk. While voluntary, it's widely adopted and often referenced in regulations.
keyPoints: Five core functions: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
Provides common language for cybersecurity
Applicable to organisations of all sizes
Complements ISA/IEC 62443 standards
Often required by regulations and contracts

sections.title: Network Security Basics
sections.description: Network security principles, technologies, and their application in IACS
learningObjectives: Identify key principles of network security

topics.title: Network Security Principles
topics.definition: Network security principles are foundational concepts that guide the design and implementation of secure networks.
topics.explanation: Key principles include defence in depth (multiple layers of security), least privilege (minimum necessary access), and network segmentation (isolating critical systems). These principles help organisations protect networks from various threats.
keyPoints: Defence in depth: Multiple security layers
Least privilege: Minimum necessary access
Network segmentation: Isolating critical systems
Monitoring and logging: Detecting suspicious activity
Regular updates and patching: Closing vulnerabilities

topics.title: Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems
topics.definition: IDS/IPS are security tools that monitor network traffic for suspicious activity and can automatically block or alert on detected threats.
topics.explanation: IDS (Intrusion Detection System) detects suspicious activity and alerts administrators. IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) can automatically block detected threats. Both have limitations in IACS environments where they must not interfere with critical operations.
keyPoints: IDS monitors and alerts on suspicious activity
IPS can automatically block threats
Both use signature-based and anomaly-based detection
Limitations in IACS: Cannot disrupt critical operations
Must be carefully tuned to avoid false positives

sections.title: Industrial Protocols
sections.description: Overview of industrial protocols used in IACS systems
learningObjectives: Define and give examples of industrial protocols
Explain MODBUS protocol structure and communication model

topics.title: Industrial Protocols Overview
topics.definition: Industrial protocols are standardised communication methods used by devices in industrial automation systems to exchange data and commands.
topics.explanation: Different protocols serve different purposes. MODBUS is a simple master-slave protocol. PROFIBUS is used in manufacturing. OPC provides standardised data exchange. Understanding these protocols is essential for securing IACS systems.
keyPoints: MODBUS: Simple, widely used, limited security
PROFIBUS: Manufacturing-focused, deterministic
OPC: Standardised data exchange, multiple variants
Ethernet/IP: Industrial Ethernet protocol
Many protocols were designed for functionality, not security

topics.title: MODBUS Protocol
topics.definition: MODBUS is a simple, open-source industrial protocol that uses a master-slave communication model for data exchange between devices.
topics.explanation: MODBUS was developed in 1979 and is widely used due to its simplicity. It operates on serial or Ethernet connections. However, it lacks built-in security features, making it vulnerable to attacks if not properly protected.
keyPoints: Master-slave communication model
Simple request-response protocol
No built-in authentication or encryption
Widely used in legacy systems
Must be protected with network segmentation and firewalls

sections.title: Introduction to Patch Management
sections.description: Patch management strategies and requirements for IACS
learningObjectives: Explain how IACS patching protects against malware
Identify asset owner and supplier patching requirements
Understand patch management challenges in IACS

topics.title: IACS Patch Management
topics.definition: Patch management is the process of regularly updating software and firmware to fix security vulnerabilities and improve system performance.
topics.explanation: Patches address known vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit. In IACS environments, patch management is challenging because systems often cannot be taken offline for updates. Organisations must balance security with operational requirements.
keyPoints: Patches fix security vulnerabilities
Critical patches should be applied quickly
Testing is essential before applying patches
Downtime must be minimized in IACS
Some legacy systems cannot be patched

sections.title: Security Risk Assessment for System Design
sections.description: Risk assessment methodology and system design for IACS
learningObjectives: Design systems based on risk assessment

topics.title: Security Risk Assessment
topics.definition: Security risk assessment is a systematic process of identifying threats, vulnerabilities, and their potential impact to determine appropriate security controls.
topics.explanation: Risk assessment involves identifying what assets need protection, what threats exist, what vulnerabilities could be exploited, and what the consequences would be. The result is a prioritised list of risks that guides security investments.
keyPoints: Identify critical assets and systems
Identify potential threats and threat actors
Identify vulnerabilities that could be exploited
Assess likelihood and impact of incidents
Prioritise risks for mitigation

sections.title: Security Programme Requirements for IACS Service Providers
sections.description: Security requirements for system integrators, consultants, and service providers

topics.title: Service Provider Security Programmes
topics.definition: Service providers (system integrators, consultants, maintenance providers) must implement security programmes to protect customer systems and data.
topics.explanation: Service providers have access to critical customer systems, making them attractive targets for attackers. They must implement security programmes that protect customer data, ensure secure development practices, and maintain security throughout the service relationship.
keyPoints: Service providers must protect customer data
Secure development practices are essential
Personnel security and background checks are important
Supply chain security must be managed
Incident response procedures must be established

sections.title: Developing Secure Products & Services
sections.description: Secure development practices for IACS products and services
learningObjectives: Implement security in design and development

topics.title: Secure Development Practices
topics.definition: Secure development practices are methodologies and processes that integrate security throughout the software and product development lifecycle.
topics.explanation: Security should not be an afterthought added at the end of development. Instead, it should be considered from the initial design phase through deployment and maintenance. This includes threat modelling, secure coding practices, security testing, and vulnerability management.
keyPoints: Security must be designed in, not added on
Threat modelling identifies potential attacks
Secure coding practices prevent common vulnerabilities
Security testing verifies controls are effective
Vulnerability management addresses discovered issues

sections.title: Security Profiles for ISA 62443
sections.description: Security profiles and their role in defining security requirements

topics.title: ISA 62443 Security Profiles
topics.definition: A security profile is a specification of security requirements for a particular IACS system, derived from the ISA/IEC 62443 standards.
topics.explanation: Profiles are tailored to specific systems based on risk assessment and target security levels. They specify which security requirements apply and at what level of rigor. Profiles provide a bridge between generic standards and specific system implementations.
keyPoints: Profiles are derived from risk assessment
Profiles specify applicable security requirements
Profiles define the rigor of requirement implementation
Profiles guide system design and implementation
Profiles enable conformance assessment

sections.title: IACS Security Profile Scheme
sections.description: The scheme for defining and implementing security profiles

topics.title: Security Profile Scheme Framework
topics.definition: The security profile scheme is a structured approach for developing, implementing, and assessing security profiles for IACS systems.
topics.explanation: The scheme provides a systematic methodology for selecting and tailoring security requirements from ISA/IEC 62443 standards to create profiles specific to individual systems. It ensures consistency and completeness in security profile development.
keyPoints: Scheme provides structured profile development methodology
Profiles are based on risk assessment results
Profiles specify security requirements and implementation levels
Scheme enables conformance assessment
Scheme supports continuous improvement
